source_text: Οὐχὶ δὲ γένος, οὐδὲ ἀνατροφὰς σώματος ἐπαινέσων ἔρχομαι· εἶτα μέλλω καὶ ἀναβάλλομαι ὑπ᾽ εὐλαβείας περιττῆς· οὐδέ γε ἰσχὺν, ἢ κάλλος· ταῦτα δὴ τὰ τῶν μειρακίων ἐγκώμια, ὧν ἧττον φροντὶς κατ᾽ ἀξίαν τε καὶ μὴ, λεγομένων. πραγμάτων γὰρ οὐ μονίμων, οὐδὲ ἑστώτων, φθειρομένων δὲ ποικίλως, καὶ ταχέως, λόγον ποιεῖσθαί τινα σεμνοειδῶς καὶ ἀξιοπρεπῶς δὴ ταῖς ἀναβολαῖς, μὴ καὶ ψυχρὸν ἢ περιττότερον ᾖ, οὐκ ἄν μοι τούτων εἴπερ τι λέγειν προὔκειτο, ἀχρήστων μὲν ὄντων καὶ ματαίων, καὶ οἵων οὐκ ἄν ποτε ἑκὼν προὐθέμην λέγειν. οὐ μὴν ἀλλ᾽ εἴπερ προὔκειτό τι τοιοῦτον, οὐδ᾽ εἶχεν ἂν εὐλάβειαν ὁ λόγος, οὐδὲ φροντίδα, μή πῃ τι λέγων, ἥττων τῆς ἀξίας φαινοίμην. νυνὶ δὲ ὅ, τι θεοειδέστατον αὐτοῦ· καὶ ὅπερ ἐν αὐτῷ συγγενὲς ὂν τυγχάνει Θεῷ, ἐγκαθειργμένον μὲν τῷ φαινομένῳ καὶ θνητῷ τῷδε, ὅτι δὲ φιλοπονώτατα ἐξομοιοῦσθαι βιαζόμενον τῷ Θεῷ. τούτου μνημονεύων καὶ ἐφάπτεσθαί πως μέλλων πραγμάτων μειζόνων, καί τινος διὰ τούτου καὶ τῆς εἰς τὸ θεῖον εὐχαριστίας, ὅτι μοι συγκυρῆσαι, τοιούτῳ δεδώρηται ἀνδρὶ, παρὰ πᾶσάν γε τὴν ἀνθρώπων προσδοκίαν τῶν τε ἄλλων καὶ τὴν ἐμοῦ αὐτοῦ, οὔτε προτεθειμένου ποτὲ, οὔτε καὶ ἐλπίσαντος τοιούτων ἐφάπτεσθαι μέλλων, μικρὸς ὢν καὶ ἄνους παντελῶς, οὐκ εὐλόγως ἀναδύομαί τε καὶ ὀκνῶ καὶ ἑκὼν σιωπῶ.
thought_title: Not his birth or body, but the godlike part of the man
orientation: Gregory says he has come to praise not Origen's birth or body but the godlike part of the man, and so he shrinks from the task.
pass_a_gloss: Not birth/family, not nurture of body am I coming to praise; then [if so] I delay and put off from excessive scruple; nor strength or beauty: these the encomia of youths, about which less concern whether spoken worthily or not. For to make a λόγος about πράγματα not permanent nor standing, but perishing variously and quickly, with solemn appearance and with seeming dignity in delays, preambles — lest it be frigid or overdone — I would not, if I had set out to say any of these, they being useless and vain, such as I would never willingly have proposed. Nevertheless if such a thing had been proposed, the speech would have no caution nor anxiety lest in speaking I appear beneath the merit. But now: what is most godlike of him, and what in him is akin to God, shut in this visible and mortal [body], yet most laboriously forcing itself to be likened to God. Remembering this, and about to touch greater matters, and through this a thanksgiving to the divine, that it was granted me to meet such a man, beyond all expectation of men, others' and mine, I neither having proposed nor hoped to touch such things — being about to, small and senseless wholly — οὐκ εὐλόγως [read: not without reason] I shrink back, hesitate and willingly am silent.

pass_b_english: It is not his family, nor the upbringing of his body, that I have come to praise, and so hang back and delay out of excessive scruple; nor his strength or his beauty. These are the praises given to young men, and it matters little whether they are spoken worthily or not. For to make a speech about things that neither last nor stand firm, but perish quickly and in many ways, and to do it with solemn airs and a show of dignity, and with such delays, might well prove frigid or overdone. If I had set out to speak of any of these things, I would not do it that way, since they are useless and vain, and I would never willingly have chosen to speak of them. Even so, had I set out to speak of anything of that kind, my speech would have felt no caution and no anxiety that I might seem, in what I said, to fall short of what the subject deserves.

But now I am to speak of what is most godlike in him, the part of him that is akin to God: shut up in this visible and mortal frame, yet striving with all its labor to be made like God. As I call this to mind, I am about to touch in some way on greater matters, and through it on a kind of thanksgiving to God, because it has been granted me to meet such a man, beyond all human expectation, both that of others and my own. I had never proposed it, nor even hoped for it. Now that I am about to touch on such things, small as I am and wholly without understanding, I shrink back, not without reason, and hesitate, and would willingly keep silent.
notes: The print reads οὐκ εὐλόγως (literally 'not reasonably'), which contradicts the argument. The Vossius Latin column has 'non immerito subterfugio ac formido' ('not without reason I shrink and fear'), and 2.2 goes on to call silence safe, so the English follows 'not without reason'. 'εἶτα μέλλω καὶ ἀναβάλλομαι' is rendered 'and so hang back and delay': it is not such small themes that make him hesitate; for them his scruple would be excessive. The print 'οὐκ εὐλόγως' was checked on the page image (PDF 75, Greek col. A); the Latin column there reads 'non immeritò cunctor ac timeo, & silere prorsus malo'. 'Shut up in this visible and mortal frame' supplies 'frame' for the bare neuter τῷ φαινομένῳ καὶ θνητῷ τῷδε (the body). 'Thanksgiving to God' renders εἰς τὸ θεῖον ('to the divine'). Possible echo of being 'made like God' (Plato, Theaetetus 176b, ὁμοίωσις θεῷ); not Scripture, not cited.
